title: Remove a tub spout without a strap wrench
mechanism_check: A tub spout is either threaded onto a pipe nipple (twists off counterclockwise) or slip-fit over bare copper held by a set screw underneath.
Forcing the wrong type strips threads or twists the copper stub inside the wall — the failure mode is a leak you cannot reach.
Feel underneath the spout near the wall for a small hex set screw: present means slip-fit, absent means threaded.
improvised_tools: Belt or webbing strap as a strap wrench: loop around the spout, pull the tail to cinch.
Penetrating oil and patience for corroded threads.
An Allen key or improvised hex driver for the set screw.
steps: Feel under the spout near the wall for the set screw; loosen it fully if present.
If slip-fit: twist and pull straight off the copper stub. If threaded: apply the strap wrench and turn counterclockwise.
For corroded threads, soak with penetrating oil, wait 15 minutes, then turn with steady pressure — never jerk.
Clean the nipple threads and wrap with fresh tape before installing the new spout.
stop_conditions: If the in-wall pipe starts twisting with the spout, stop: you are about to break a joint inside the wall.
If the copper stub is shorter than 2 inches or deformed, stop and call a plumber — a bad cut there means opening the wall.

title: Find and work your main water shutoff before anything else
mechanism_check: Every fixture has a local stop, and the house has a main: a gate or ball valve where water enters, plus a curb stop at the meter.
Gate valves seal with a wedge that corrodes in place; ball valves seal with a quarter-turn ball and rarely freeze.
Closing the wrong valve or snapping a frozen one turns a drip into a flood.
improvised_tools: A water meter key (or large crescent wrench) for the curb stop.
A labeled tag or tape so the next person finds the main in seconds.
Penetrating oil for a valve that has not moved in years.
steps: Locate the main shutoff now, before you need it: where the line enters the house, near the meter, or in a crawlspace or basement.
Exercise it: close and reopen fully twice a year so it never freezes.
Verify it holds: close it, open a faucet, and confirm flow stops completely.
Tag it and tell everyone in the house where it is.
stop_conditions: If the valve will not close fully or leaks from the stem when you touch it, leave it and call a plumber — a broken main valve is their job.
Never force a gate valve past resistance; a snapped stem means no water until it is replaced.

title: Read your water meter to find hidden leaks
mechanism_check: The meter measures all water entering the house; with every fixture off, any movement means a leak somewhere.
Most meters have a small leak-indicator dial or triangle that spins on tiny flows the main dial will not show.
Toilets are the usual thief: a bad flapper can waste hundreds of gallons a day silently.
improvised_tools: A notebook: record the meter reading, wait two hours with no water use, read again.
Food coloring for the toilet tank test.
steps: Turn off every fixture, ice maker, and irrigation; note the meter reading and the leak indicator.
Wait two hours with zero water use, then read again — any change is a leak.
Isolate: close the toilet supply valves and repeat; if movement stops, the toilets are the leak.
Drop food coloring in each toilet tank; color in the bowl within 30 minutes means a leaking flapper.
stop_conditions: If the meter spins with the house main closed, the leak is in the service line underground — call a plumber, that is excavation.
If you cannot find the meter or the curb box is paved over, call the water utility, not a plumber.

title: Free a stuck shutoff valve without breaking it
mechanism_check: Angle stops freeze because the rubber washer bonds to the seat and the stem packing corrodes.
The weak points are the packing nut (leaks when disturbed) and the stem itself (snaps under torque).
The goal is movement, not force: patience beats leverage here.
improvised_tools: Penetrating oil, applied to the stem and left to soak.
Two wrenches: one to hold the valve body, one to turn — so torque never reaches the pipe.
A rag and a bucket, because the packing will probably weep.
steps: Shut the house main first so a broken stop is an inconvenience, not a flood.
Soak the stem with penetrating oil; wait at least 15 minutes.
Hold the valve body steady with one wrench and work the handle back and forth in small arcs.
Once it moves, run it full open to full closed twice, then leave it fully open or fully closed — never half.
stop_conditions: If the stem snaps or the packing pours water, close the house main and replace the valve — do not try to rebuild a stop under pressure.
If the pipe behind the valve starts flexing, stop: the valve is soldered or threaded to something you cannot see.

title: Seal pipe threads without Teflon tape
mechanism_check: Tapered pipe threads seal because the thread flanks wedge together; the sealant only fills the spiral leak path.
Dope, tape, and paste all do the same job: gap filler, not glue.
Over-tightening splits fittings; under-sealing weeps. The seal lives in the middle turns.
improvised_tools: Pipe dope or thread sealant paste if available (better than tape for large fittings).
Hemp fiber or cotton string with paste as a classic field substitute.
A rag to clean old sealant off threads — sealant never sticks to sealant.
steps: Clean the male threads completely; pick out old tape or dope.
Apply sealant to the male threads only, starting one thread back from the end so none enters the waterway.
Tighten hand-tight plus one to two turns with a wrench — snug, then a quarter more.
Pressurize and check; a weep gets another quarter turn, not disassembly.
stop_conditions: If a plastic female fitting cracks or the threads jump (cross-threaded), stop: back it out and start over, do not force it.
Never use improvised sealants on gas lines — gas gets proper gas-rated dope, and a pro if you are unsure.

title: Join PVC pipe with primer and cement
mechanism_check: PVC joints are not glued, they are solvent-welded: primer softens the plastic and cement fuses the two pieces into one.
The joint reaches handling strength in minutes but full cure takes hours; pressure too early blows it apart.
Dry-fit first: the pipe should bottom out in the fitting with a firm push — that interference fit is what makes the weld.
improvised_tools: PVC primer and cement matched to the pipe size — there are no substitutes for the chemistry.
A deburring knife or sandpaper for the cut edge; a dry rag.
A marker to mark insertion depth so you know the pipe seated fully.
steps: Cut square, deburr inside and out, dry-fit and mark the depth.
Prime the outside of the pipe and the inside of the fitting — glossy, no dry spots.
Brush cement on both, push together with a quarter turn, hold 30 seconds.
Wipe the bead; cure 15 minutes to handle, 2 hours before pressure on small pipe, 24 for large.
stop_conditions: If the pipe will not bottom in the dry fit, stop: wrong size or out-of-round — forcing it guarantees a bad weld.
Below freezing or in rain, solvent welding is unreliable — tent and warm the joint or wait for better conditions.

title: Clear a clogged sink or tub drain with no plunger
mechanism_check: Bathroom clogs are hair and soap matted just past the drain; kitchen clogs are grease cooled into a plug.
A plunger works by pressure pulses, not suction — anything that makes a seal and moves water does the same job.
Chemical drain openers eat pipes and traps before they eat clogs; mechanical removal always comes first.
improvised_tools: A plastic bottle with the bottom cut off, pressed over the drain as a bellows.
Baking soda plus vinegar followed by boiling water for grease.
A straightened wire coat hanger with a small hook for hair.
steps: Remove the stopper or strainer; pull out all reachable hair and gunk by hand or hook.
Seal the overflow with a wet rag, fill the basin with 2 inches of water.
Press the cut bottle over the drain and pump hard 10 to 15 times — same physics as a plunger.
For grease: half a cup of baking soda, half a cup of vinegar, wait 15 minutes, flush with a kettle of boiling water.
stop_conditions: If multiple fixtures back up at once, stop: that is a main-line blockage — no DIY chemical or tool fixes it.
If a chemical opener was already used, do not plunge or snake: wear gloves and eye protection, the splash burns.

title: Clean a P-trap by hand
mechanism_check: The P-trap is the U-bend under the sink; it holds a water plug that blocks sewer gas, and it is where clogs settle.
Trap nuts are hand-tight plastic or chrome; over-tightening cracks them.
Everything above the trap is your mess to catch in a bucket — plan for it.
improvised_tools: A bucket and old towels under the trap.
Channel-lock pliers or a strap for a stubborn slip nut — hand-tight is the spec.
A bottle brush or rag to scrub the trap walls.
steps: Place the bucket under the trap; loosen both slip nuts by hand (counterclockwise).
Drop the trap out, dump it, and scrub out the sludge — check the tailpiece for the clog too.
Reseat the washers (tapered side toward the nut), hand-tighten the nuts, then a quarter turn.
Run water and check both joints for drips.
stop_conditions: If the slip nuts are corroded metal and crumble, stop and replace the whole trap — rebuilding corroded chrome is a leak factory.
If the wall pipe (trap arm) moves when you loosen the nut, stop: the in-wall connection is compromised.

title: Diagnose a running toilet
mechanism_check: A toilet runs for two reasons: water leaks from tank to bowl (bad flapper) or water never stops entering (bad fill valve).
The overflow tube sets the max level; if the fill valve lets water rise into it, the toilet runs forever by design.
Diagnosis is free and takes five minutes; parts are cheap — never replace parts before diagnosing.
improvised_tools: Food coloring or a dark drink for the tank-to-bowl test.
Your eyes: watch the water level relative to the overflow tube.
steps: Take the tank lid off and watch: if water flows into the overflow tube, the fill valve is the culprit.
If the level is below the tube, add dye to the tank and wait 15 minutes without flushing — color in the bowl means the flapper leaks.
Push down on the flapper: if the running stops, it is the flapper or its chain, not the fill valve.
Fix the one failed part — flapper or fill valve — not both blindly.
stop_conditions: If the tank itself is cracked or the porcelain is crazed around the bolts, stop: replace the toilet, no part fixes cracked porcelain.
If water is coming from the supply line or shutoff rather than inside the tank, that is a different repair — shut the valve and fix the supply.

title: Fix a toilet flapper and chain
mechanism_check: The flapper is a rubber seal over the flush valve; the chain connects it to the handle with a little slack.
Too tight a chain holds the flapper open; too loose and it tangles under the flapper; a warped flapper never seals.
Chlorine and age eat flappers in 3 to 5 years — it is a wear item, not a failure.
improvised_tools: A universal flapper — note the flush valve size (2 vs 3 inch) before buying.
Scissors to trim the chain to length.
steps: Shut the toilet supply, flush to empty the tank, unhook the old flapper from the overflow pegs.
Wipe the flush valve seat clean — grit under the new flapper leaks like the old one did.
Hook the new flapper on, connect the chain with about half an inch of slack.
Turn the water on, flush twice, and do the dye test to confirm the seal.
stop_conditions: If the flush valve seat is pitted or cracked, a new flapper will not seal — replace the whole flush valve or the toilet.
If the tank bolts spin or the tank wobbles, stop: the gasket under the tank is suspect — that is a tank-pull job.

title: Replace a toilet fill valve
mechanism_check: The fill valve refills the tank and sets the water level via a float; modern ones are a single tower that twists to height.
It connects under the tank with one plastic locknut — the only seal that matters is the gasket under that nut.
Water level should sit about an inch below the overflow tube.
improvised_tools: A universal fill valve — one part fits nearly everything.
A sponge and towel; the tank never fully drains by flushing.
steps: Shut the supply, flush, sponge out the remaining tank water, disconnect the supply line.
Unscrew the locknut under the tank, lift out the old valve, drop in the new one at the right height.
Hand-tighten the locknut, reconnect the supply line and the refill tube to the overflow.
Turn water on slowly, set the level an inch below the overflow, flush and verify it shuts off.
stop_conditions: If the tank's valve hole is cracked or the porcelain around it is damaged, stop — the tank is done.
If the supply line or shutoff leaks when disturbed, fix that first before blaming the new valve.

title: Restore a weak toilet flush
mechanism_check: Flush power comes from water rushing through rim jets and the siphon jet; mineral scale chokes the rim jets first.
A weak flush is almost never the flapper — it is low tank level or clogged jets.
The siphon jet is the big hole at the front bottom of the bowl; if it is scaled shut, the siphon never starts.
improvised_tools: A piece of wire or an Allen key to poke out rim jets.
White vinegar and a few hours of soak time for scale.
A hand mirror to inspect under the rim.
steps: Confirm the tank fills to the marked line — low level is the cheapest fix.
Poke each rim jet clear with the wire, working around the whole rim.
Pour a gallon of vinegar into the overflow tube and let it sit overnight to dissolve scale.
Flush and compare; a strong swirl means the jets were the problem.
stop_conditions: If the bowl has a partial main-line clog (water rises then slowly drains), stop: that is a drain problem, not a flush problem.
If the toilet is an ancient 3.5-gallon bowl with chronic trouble, the honest fix is replacement, not more descaling.

title: Replace a toilet wax ring
mechanism_check: The wax ring is the only seal between the toilet horn and the floor flange; it compresses once and never reseals.
Any rocking, any flange below floor level, or any sewer smell at the base means the ring has failed.
This job is 90 percent careful lifting and resetting — the ring itself costs a few dollars.
improvised_tools: A new wax ring (or waxless silicone seal — more forgiving for beginners).
New closet bolts and a putty knife; rags to plug the open drain.
A second person: toilets are heavy and awkward, not technically hard.
steps: Shut supply, flush, sponge the tank and bowl dry, disconnect the supply line.
Rock the toilet gently to break the old wax seal, then lift straight up and set it on rags.
Scrape the flange clean, set new bolts, press the new ring onto the flange.
Lower the toilet straight down onto the bolts, sit on it to compress, then tighten bolts evenly — snug, never torqued.
stop_conditions: If the flange is cracked or sits more than a quarter inch below the floor, stop: the flange needs repair or a spacer before any ring will seal.
If the subfloor around the flange is soft or rotted, stop: that is structural repair first, toilet second.

title: Replace a toilet supply line
mechanism_check: The supply line runs from the shutoff to the fill valve; old lines fail at the crimp or the cone washer.
It is a compression seal: the washer or ferrule does the work, not thread torque.
Replace it any time you disturb it — a ten-year-old line owes you nothing.
improvised_tools: A braided stainless supply line in the right length and thread size (7/8 ballcock is standard).
A small bowl and towel for the residual water.
steps: Shut the angle stop, flush, and hold a bowl under the valve while you unscrew the line at both ends.
Inspect the shutoff outlet threads; clean off the old washer remnants.
Hand-thread the new line onto the valve, then the fill valve — hand-tight plus a quarter turn.
Open the valve slowly and check both ends dry.
stop_conditions: If the angle stop itself leaks or will not fully close, replace the stop first — a new line on a bad valve still floods.
If the fill valve threads are cracked plastic, stop: the fill valve needs replacing, not the line.

title: Clear a toilet clog with a closet auger
mechanism_check: A closet auger is a 3 to 6 foot cable in a tube with a crank; the tube's bend aims the cable through the toilet trap.
It breaks up or hooks the clog inside the toilet's own trap — it does not reach the main line.
The porcelain scratches if the tube's boot is not seated; the crank works by steady rotation, not force.
improvised_tools: A closet auger (the one plumbing tool worth owning for every house).
Rubber gloves and old towels; this is a wet job.
steps: Seat the auger's curved tube fully into the bowl outlet so the boot protects the porcelain.
Crank clockwise while feeding the cable until you feel resistance.
Work the crank back and forth through the resistance — you are breaking up or snagging the clog.
Retract, flush, and repeat once; two passes clear nearly every toilet-trap clog.
stop_conditions: If the auger passes freely but the bowl still will not drain, the clog is past the toilet — stop and snake from a cleanout or call a pro.
If you feel the cable kink or bind hard, stop cranking: a kinked cable can crack the trap.

title: Unclog a toilet with no plunger
mechanism_check: A plunger works by pressure pulses against a sealed bowl; the seal matters more than the tool.
Hot water softens organic clogs; dish soap lubricates the trap.
Time is a tool: a clog that will not move in five minutes often dissolves in thirty.
improvised_tools: Dish soap and the hottest tap water (not boiling — boiling water can crack porcelain).
Cling film stretched tight over the bowl as a membrane plunger.
A mop head in a plastic bag as a last-resort bellows.
steps: Squeeze a generous squirt of dish soap into the bowl and let it sink for 10 minutes.
Pour in a bucket of hot (not boiling) water from waist height; wait 20 to 30 minutes.
If it has not cleared, stretch cling film airtight across the bowl rim and press the center down sharply, repeatedly.
Flush only when the water level has dropped on its own.
stop_conditions: If the bowl is brim-full and rising, do not flush again — bail water out first or you will flood the floor.
If sewage backs up into the tub or shower when you flush, stop: that is a main-line blockage, call a pro.

title: Stop a dripping compression faucet
mechanism_check: A compression faucet seals when the stem washer presses onto the valve seat; drips mean the washer is worn or the seat is pitted.
Each full turn of the handle is the stem traveling down — the washer is a consumable, the seat is the permanent part.
Always fix the washer first; only touch the seat if a new washer still drips.
improvised_tools: An assortment of flat faucet washers and O-rings.
A seat wrench, or patience to reseat with a dressing tool.
Plumber's grease for the stem threads.
steps: Shut both fixture stops (or the house main), open the faucet to release pressure.
Pull the handle and bonnet nut, unscrew the stem, and swap the washer on its screw.
Feel the seat with a fingertip: smooth means reassemble; rough means dress or replace the seat.
Grease the stem, reassemble, and pressurize — the drip should be gone.
stop_conditions: If the seat is cracked or the faucet body is split, stop: the faucet needs replacing, not rebuilding.
If the bonnet nut is frozen and the whole faucet body twists, stop — you will break the supply connections.

title: Replace a faucet cartridge without the puller
mechanism_check: Cartridge faucets (single-handle) seal with a ceramic or plastic cartridge that lifts and rotates; scale and mineral bond it to the brass body.
The puller exists because yanking cocks the cartridge sideways and cracks the housing.
Straight-out force with even pressure is the whole trick — the tool just guarantees the geometry.
improvised_tools: Penetrating oil or white vinegar to dissolve the mineral bond.
Two flat tools (putty knives or screwdrivers) used as opposing levers under the cartridge ears.
A rag to protect the finish.
steps: Shut the stops, remove the handle and retaining nut or clip.
Soak the cartridge base with vinegar or penetrating oil; wait 15 minutes.
Lever gently and evenly from two sides, rocking the cartridge straight out — never pry from one side only.
Clean the housing bore, grease the new cartridge's O-rings, and press it straight in.
stop_conditions: If the cartridge breaks off leaving the stem inside, stop: extracting a broken stem without the tool risks the housing — call a pro.
If the brass housing is cracked or dezincified (pink, crumbly), the faucet is done — replace it.

title: Replace a kitchen faucet
mechanism_check: The faucet mounts through the sink deck with a shank nut underneath; supply lines and the sprayer hose connect below.
Under-sink work is all by feel in a dark cabinet — layout and lighting are the job.
The deck seal (putty or gasket) is what keeps countertop water out of the cabinet.
improvised_tools: A basin wrench (or a deep socket on an extension) for the shank nuts.
A headlamp — non-negotiable under a sink.
Plumber's putty or the supplied gasket for the deck seal.
steps: Shut both stops, disconnect supplies and sprayer, and photograph the layout before touching anything.
Remove the shank nuts from below, lift the old faucet out, and clean the deck.
Set the new faucet with its gasket or a rope of putty, tighten the shank nuts evenly from below.
Reconnect supplies (new braided lines), run both hot and cold, and check every joint dry.
stop_conditions: If the shutoff valves leak or will not close, replace them first — installing a faucet you cannot isolate is asking for a flood.
If the sink deck is rusted through around the holes, stop: the sink needs replacing, not the faucet.

title: Install a bathroom lavatory faucet
mechanism_check: Same physics as a kitchen faucet on a smaller scale: shank nuts, deck seal, supply connections — plus a pop-up drain to link.
Centerset (4-inch) vs widespread (8-inch) is decided by the sink's hole spacing; measure before buying.
The pop-up rod linkage is the fiddly part: small adjustments make it seal or leak.
improvised_tools: Basin wrench, headlamp, putty or gasket as with any faucet.
A small adjustable wrench for the pop-up pivot nut.
steps: Confirm hole spacing matches the faucet; shut the stops.
Set the faucet with gasket or putty, tighten shank nuts evenly from below.
Install the pop-up drain: putty under the flange, pivot rod through the tailpiece, clip to the lift rod.
Connect supplies, adjust the lift rod so the stopper seals fully, test hot and cold.
stop_conditions: If the drain tailpiece or trap does not line up with the new faucet's drain, stop and replan the trap — do not force misaligned plastic.
Same rule as kitchen: bad stops or a rusted deck stop the job.

title: Clean a faucet aerator to restore flow
mechanism_check: The aerator is the screen at the spout tip; it mixes air into the stream and catches every grain of sediment in the line.
Low flow at one faucet while others are fine is almost always the aerator.
It unscrews counterclockwise; the parts stack in a specific order — note it as you take it apart.
improvised_tools: A rag for grip (protects the chrome), a small bowl of vinegar.
An old toothbrush for the screen.
steps: Unscrew the aerator by hand with a rag for grip; note the order of screen, mixer, and washer.
Tap out the debris and soak the parts in vinegar 30 minutes; scrub the screen.
Reassemble in the same order and thread it back on hand-tight.
If flow is still weak, run the faucet without the aerator to confirm the restriction was there.
stop_conditions: If the aerator housing is cracked or the threads are stripped, replace it — they cost a few dollars.
If flow stays weak with the aerator off, the restriction is upstream (supply line or valve) — different repair.

title: Replace a showerhead
mechanism_check: The showerhead threads onto a shower arm; the seal is a washer inside the head's nut, not the threads.
Teflon tape on the arm threads plus the washer is belt and suspenders.
The arm itself threads into a fitting in the wall — torque on the arm travels straight into that hidden joint.
improvised_tools: A rag to protect the finish while gripping; Teflon tape.
A spare rubber washer — the old one is usually flattened dead.
steps: Hold the shower arm steady with one hand (or a wrench on a rag) and unscrew the old head.
Clean the arm threads, wrap 3 to 4 turns of tape clockwise, seat a fresh washer in the new head.
Thread the new head on hand-tight plus a quarter turn.
Run the shower and check the joint — a drip gets a quarter turn more, not more tape.
stop_conditions: If the shower arm turns in the wall or wobbles, stop: the in-wall fitting is loose — tightening the head will make it worse.
If the arm is corroded thin, replace the arm too; a new head on a rotten arm is a leak waiting.

title: Repair a tub and shower diverter
mechanism_check: The diverter is the gate or pin you lift on the tub spout; it blocks the spout so water takes the shower riser.
A worn gate lets most water fall from the spout while the shower dribbles — it is a seal problem, not pressure.
Many diverters are part of the spout itself: replacing the spout replaces the diverter.
improvised_tools: Vinegar soak for a sticky gate; a replacement spout if the gate is worn.
The same strap-wrench improvisation as spout removal.
steps: Test: run the tub, lift the diverter — if more than a trickle still comes from the spout, the gate is worn.
Try descaling first: soak the spout in vinegar to free a sticky gate.
If the shower still starves, replace the spout — the diverter comes with it.
For a three-handle valve with a separate diverter stem, rebuild it like a compression faucet.
stop_conditions: If the shower riser pipe inside the wall is the leak (water in the wall, not at the spout), stop: that is a wall-open repair.
If a pressure-balance valve cartridge is failing, that is a cartridge replacement — do not force the diverter.

title: Fix a bathroom sink pop-up drain
mechanism_check: The pop-up stopper pivots on a ball rod through the tailpiece; the lift rod pulls it via a clevis strap.
Slow drains here are hair wrapped on the stopper; a stopper that will not seal is a misadjusted linkage.
The pivot nut seal is the only thing between you and a cabinet flood — snug it, do not crush it.
improvised_tools: A small adjustable wrench for the pivot nut.
Needle-nose pliers for the clevis clip.
steps: Pull the stopper out and clear the hair — this fixes most slow pop-ups.
To adjust the seal: squeeze the clevis spring clip and move it up or down the lift rod until the stopper seats.
Snug the pivot nut just enough to stop drips; the rod must still pivot freely.
Test with a full basin: it should hold water, then release completely.
stop_conditions: If the pivot ball or tailpiece threads are corroded through, replace the whole pop-up assembly — adjustments will not save it.
If the tailpiece is plastic and cracked at the pivot hole, stop: replace, do not patch.

title: Replace a kitchen sink basket strainer
mechanism_check: The strainer seals to the sink with plumber's putty and clamps from below with a locknut or retainer.
Leaks at the strainer rim mean the putty seal failed, not the strainer.
Putty stays soft and seals by compression — it needs a full, even squeeze-out.
improvised_tools: Plumber's putty (not silicone — putty is removable next time).
A strainer wrench or large pliers for the locknut; a second person or a stick to hold the strainer from above.
steps: Disconnect the tailpiece, loosen the locknut from below, and push the old strainer up and out.
Scrape the sink opening clean; roll a rope of putty and press it around the new strainer's lip.
Drop it in, have a helper hold it (or wedge it), and tighten the locknut evenly until putty squeezes out all around.
Trim the squeeze-out, reconnect the tailpiece, and fill the sink to test.
stop_conditions: If the sink opening is rusted or the stainless is thin and flexing, a new strainer will not seal — the sink is the problem.
On a garbage-disposal side, align the disposal first; forcing the strainer to meet a hung disposal cracks the mount.

title: Reseal tub and sink caulk
mechanism_check: Caulk is the flexible gasket between dissimilar materials (tub to tile); grout is rigid and cracks there.
New caulk never sticks to old caulk or soap film — removal and cleaning is the job, application is the finish.
A tooled concave bead sheds water; a proud blob traps it.
improvised_tools: A utility knife and plastic scraper for the old bead; rubbing alcohol for the final wipe.
Painter's tape for clean lines; a fingertip or spoon for tooling.
steps: Cut out all the old caulk — every bit; wipe the joint with alcohol and let it dry completely.
Fill the tub with water first so the joint is at its widest when you caulk it.
Tape both sides, lay a smooth bead of 100 percent silicone, tool it concave in one pass, and pull the tape immediately.
Let it cure 24 hours before wetting.
stop_conditions: If the tub moves or the wall flexes when you lean on it, caulk is a bandage — the movement will crack any bead; fix the support first.
If there is mold or soft drywall behind the old caulk, stop: that is a tear-out repair, not a recaulk.

title: Patch a pinhole leak in copper pipe
mechanism_check: Pinholes are pitting corrosion from the inside out; the visible drip is the tip of a thinned section.
A patch clamps over the hole, but the pipe around it is still thin — this buys time, not permanence.
Rubber plus a hose clamp makes a gasket; the clamp's even pressure is the seal.
improvised_tools: A piece of rubber (old hose, inner tube) and two hose clamps — or a purpose-made repair clamp.
Sandpaper to clean the pipe so the rubber seats.
Epoxy putty as a backup for weeping joints.
steps: Shut the water and dry the pipe; sand the area around the pinhole clean.
Wrap the rubber patch over the hole, center a hose clamp on each side of it.
Tighten evenly — firm, not crushing; the rubber should bulge slightly at the edges.
Restore pressure and watch for 10 minutes; plan the permanent section replacement soon.
stop_conditions: If the pipe is green and pitted over a long section, stop patching: replace the run — it is all thin.
If the leak is at a soldered joint rather than mid-pipe, a clamp will not hold reliably — plan a re-solder or a push-fit section.

title: Make a temporary repair on a burst pipe
mechanism_check: A burst is a split from freezing or a blown joint; water comes out under full pressure.
First priority is always stopping the water (main shutoff), second is a repair that holds until the permanent fix.
Push-fit fittings and repair couplings hold full pressure without tools — the legitimate temp-to-permanent bridge.
improvised_tools: A push-fit repair coupling sized to the pipe — the one fitting worth keeping on the truck.
A pipe cutter or hacksaw; sandpaper or a deburring tool.
Towels and a bucket — the line will drain when you cut it.
steps: Shut the main, open the lowest faucet to drain the line, and cut out the burst section with clean square cuts.
Deburr and clean both ends; mark the insertion depth on each.
Push the repair coupling fully onto one end, then slide it to cover the other — both marks must disappear inside.
Restore water slowly and check; push-fit is code-approved, so temporary can become permanent if the pipe is sound.
stop_conditions: If the pipe is frozen solid elsewhere, do not restore pressure until it thaws — the next burst is already waiting.
If the burst is in a wall you cannot access cleanly, stop cutting: open the wall properly or call a pro.

title: Use push-fit fittings for a no-solder emergency repair
mechanism_check: Push-fit fittings grip with stainless teeth and seal with an O-ring; depth of insertion is the whole joint.
They work on copper, PEX, and CPVC — the transition fitting in an emergency.
The pipe end must be round, clean, and deburred, or the O-ring never seals.
improvised_tools: Push-fit couplings and elbows in common sizes (1/2 and 3/4).
A depth gauge or marker; the fitting usually includes one.
A proper pipe cutter — a ragged hacksaw cut defeats the O-ring.
steps: Cut the pipe square, deburr inside and out, and clean off all corrosion.
Mark the insertion depth on the pipe.
Push straight in with a firm twist until the mark disappears into the fitting.
Tug-test it, pressurize, and check — then leave the removal tool with the homeowner if it is their house.
stop_conditions: If the pipe end is out-of-round or deeply pitted, the O-ring cannot seal — cut back to sound pipe or stop.
Push-fit is water only, and check local code for concealed use — never gas.

title: Join copper with compression fittings and no solder
mechanism_check: A compression fitting seals when the nut crushes a brass ferrule onto the pipe — the ferrule's bite is the seal.
It needs a clean, round, burr-free pipe end; the nut needs exactly enough torque to set the ferrule, then it holds.
Unlike solder, it is removable and reusable a few times — the honest no-flame copper joint.
improvised_tools: Compression couplings, elbows, or stops in the pipe size.
Two wrenches: one to hold the fitting body, one to turn the nut.
Sandpaper for the pipe end.
steps: Cut square, deburr, and polish the pipe end clean.
Slide the nut then the ferrule onto the pipe, seat the pipe fully into the fitting.
Hold the body with one wrench; tighten the nut firmly — about one full turn past hand-tight for 1/2 inch.
Pressurize and check; a weep gets an eighth turn more, then stop.
stop_conditions: If the pipe is thin or work-hardened and the ferrule will not bite, stop: the pipe needs replacing, not a tighter nut.
Never reuse a ferrule that has been fully compressed — it will not bite twice.

title: Sweat a copper joint: solder basics
mechanism_check: Soldering is capillary action: flux cleans the metal, heat draws molten solder into the joint — the solder follows the heat.
The joint must be bone-dry; one drop of water turns to steam and blows the solder out.
Overheating burns the flux and oxidizes the copper — then nothing sticks.
improvised_tools: Propane torch, lead-free solder, and flux — the non-negotiable trio.
Sandpaper or emery cloth, a fitting brush, and a spray bottle for nearby wood.
A heat shield for work near studs.
steps: Cut, deburr, sand the pipe bright and brush the fitting interior; apply a thin flux coat to both.
Assemble, heat the fitting evenly — not the solder — until the flux sizzles quiet.
Touch solder to the joint opposite the flame; when it melts and wicks in, feed until a full ring shows, then stop.
Let it cool undisturbed; wipe the joint and pressure-test.
stop_conditions: If water keeps seeping into the joint, stop: dam it or drain the line properly — steam blows every joint.
If there is wood, insulation, or old scorch nearby, stop and shield it: most soldering fires start from just one more joint.

title: Cut copper pipe without a tubing cutter
mechanism_check: A tubing cutter works by rolling a wheel around the pipe, displacing metal inward — a hacksaw removes a kerf instead.
Either way the requirements are the same: square cut, no burrs, round pipe.
A hacksaw cut needs more cleanup but makes the same joint.
improvised_tools: A fine-tooth hacksaw (32 TPI) and a steady hand.
Sandpaper and a round file for deburring.
A wrap of tape as a cut guide line.
steps: Mark the cut line all the way around with tape.
Saw lightly, rotating the pipe, letting the teeth do the work — pressure ovals the pipe.
File the outside edge and ream the inside burr completely — the burr causes turbulence and erosion.
Check the end is square and round before fitting.
stop_conditions: If the pipe ovals or kinks, cut it off and start over — an oval end never seals in compression or push-fit.
If you are cutting into a line you cannot fully drain, stop: cutting a pressurized line is a flood.

title: Connect PEX without a crimp tool
mechanism_check: PEX connections seal by compressing the pipe wall against an insert; the ring or clamp supplies the force.
Push-fit and cinch-clamp systems need no proprietary expander — the tool is convenience, not physics.
The insert must go in to full depth; a shallow insert blows off under pressure.
improvised_tools: Push-fit PEX fittings, or barbed fittings with stainless cinch clamps.
A PEX cutter (or sharp utility knife with a square cut) — the cut must be clean.
steps: Cut the PEX square and clean; slide any clamp or sleeve on before the fitting.
Push the pipe fully onto the insert to the depth mark.
Position the cinch clamp 1/8 inch from the pipe end and tighten fully — or push the push-fit home.
Pressure-test before closing the wall.
stop_conditions: If the PEX is kinked, cut the kink out — a kink is a future split, and no fitting fixes it.
Do not mix PEX-A expansion fittings with PEX-B pipe (or vice versa) without checking compatibility.

title: Transition between copper and PEX in a repair
mechanism_check: Copper and PEX have different outside diameters and different joining physics — the transition fitting is a hybrid with a copper side and a PEX side.
Dielectric corrosion is not the issue here (both are non-ferrous); mechanical grip on each side is.
The repair is only as good as the sound pipe on both sides — cut back to clean material.
improvised_tools: A copper-to-PEX transition coupling (push-fit or sweat-by-crimp).
Both joining kits: cutter, deburrer, and whichever fastening the fitting needs.
steps: Cut both pipes back to sound, round, clean material.
Prepare each end for its own system: solder-clean the copper, square-cut the PEX.
Make the copper joint first (it needs heat and stillness), then the PEX side.
Support the transition within a foot on each side — dissimilar stiffness flexes at the joint.
stop_conditions: If either side is too short to work after cutting back to sound pipe, stop: open more access instead of stretching a joint.
If the copper side is paper-thin from corrosion, the transition just moves the failure — replace the copper run.

title: Remove a stuck cleanout plug
mechanism_check: Cleanout plugs are large threaded caps, often brass or plastic in cast iron; years of corrosion weld the threads.
The plug's square or hex head is the weak point — it rounds off or snaps before the threads give.
Penetration and shock beat torque: a sharp hammer tap breaks the corrosion bond that steady force will not.
improvised_tools: A large wrench or cleanout key that fits the head fully — partial contact rounds it.
Penetrating oil and a hammer for shock.
A replacement plug on hand before you start — the old one may not survive.
steps: Soak the threads with penetrating oil; give the plug head sharp hammer taps to shock the corrosion.
Fit the wrench fully onto the head and apply steady pressure — never sudden jerks.
If the head rounds, chisel a slot and use a large screwdriver, or drill and use an extractor.
Clean the threads and install the new plug with thread sealant, hand-tight plus a quarter turn.
stop_conditions: If the cleanout body or the pipe it is threaded into starts moving, stop immediately: breaking the hub means a major repair.
If sewage is under pressure behind the plug (bulging, seeping), do not open it — call a pro with the right containment.

title: Snake a drain with a coat hanger
mechanism_check: A hanger is a stiff wire hook — it fishes hair and retrieves objects, it does not auger through grease.
Its reach is about two feet past the drain; anything deeper needs a real snake.
The hook must be small and smooth — a sharp end scratches porcelain and plastic.
improvised_tools: A wire coat hanger, straightened, with a small smooth hook bent at the end.
Pliers to form the hook; a rag to protect the drain finish.
steps: Remove the stopper or strainer; feed the hook end into the drain.
Twist and push gently past the trap bend; when you feel the clog, rotate to snag it.
Pull out slowly — most bathroom clogs come out as a single hair mass.
Flush with hot water to clear what the hook loosened.
stop_conditions: If the hanger will not pass the trap or meets solid resistance deep in, stop: forcing it can puncture a plastic trap or push the clog deeper.
If the drain has a chemical opener in it, do not fish by hand — gloves and eye protection, or wait.

title: Stop water hammer in banging pipes
mechanism_check: Water hammer is momentum: a fast-closing valve stops moving water instantly, and the shock wave bangs the pipes.
Air chambers (capped vertical stubs) absorb the shock until they waterlog; mechanical arrestors do not.
Loose pipe straps turn a small shock into a loud bang — securing the pipe is half the fix.
improvised_tools: Pipe straps or cushioned clamps to secure loose runs.
A screw-on water hammer arrestor for the offending valve.
A pressure gauge — high pressure makes hammer worse.
steps: Find the valve that triggers the bang (flush, then listen for which fixture causes it).
Strap down any loose pipe in the run — most hammer noise is actually pipe movement.
Drain the system to recharge old air chambers, or screw an arrestor onto the washing machine or dishwasher valve.
Check house pressure; over 80 PSI, the hammer will not stay fixed without a PRV.
stop_conditions: If banging comes with discolored water or pressure swings at every fixture, stop: that is a supply-side problem — call the utility or a plumber.
If pipes bang inside a finished wall you cannot open, an arrestor at the fixture is the practical fix — do not tear open walls on a guess.

title: Tame high water pressure with a PRV
mechanism_check: A pressure-reducing valve throttles the main down to a set pressure via a spring and diaphragm.
Over 80 PSI destroys washers, fill valves, and water heaters early; under 40 feels like a trickle.
A failed PRV either creeps (pressure rises at night) or chokes (pressure drops under flow) — the gauge tells you which.
improvised_tools: A hose-bib pressure gauge — the ten-dollar diagnostic that settles every pressure argument.
A PRV matched to the main size, plus unions so the next swap takes minutes.
steps: Screw the gauge on a hose bibb: static pressure over 80 PSI means you need (or need to adjust) a PRV.
Check pressure under flow (run a tub): a big drop means the PRV is undersized or failing.
Adjust the PRV bolt: clockwise raises, counterclockwise lowers — a quarter turn at a time, then recheck.
Target 50 to 60 PSI; add an expansion tank at the water heater if the system is now closed.
stop_conditions: If the PRV is seized, leaking, or the adjustment does nothing, replace it — do not force the bolt.
If there is no PRV and the main is old galvanized, stop and plan the whole entry: cutting into a corroded main is a pro job.

title: Unjam a garbage disposal without the wrench
mechanism_check: A jammed disposal is a stuck flywheel — usually a bone, utensil, or glass wedged between the plate and the shredder ring.
The hex socket underneath turns the flywheel manually; the red reset button trips on overload.
Never put a hand in the disposal — the mechanism does not care whose hand it is.
improvised_tools: A 1/4-inch Allen key (the standard disposal wrench size) or a wooden broom handle from above.
Tongs or pliers to fish out the jam object.
The reset button — always press it after clearing.
steps: Turn the wall switch OFF and unplug the disposal (or kill the breaker) — verify it is dead.
From underneath, work the Allen key back and forth in the hex socket until the flywheel spins free.
Fish out the jam object with tongs; press the red reset button.
Restore power, run cold water, and test — grinding that fades in seconds is normal.
stop_conditions: If the motor hums but the flywheel will not budge after working it, the motor is seized — replace the disposal.
If the disposal leaks from the bottom housing (not the connections), the internal seal is gone — replace, do not repair.

title: Hook up a dishwasher with an air gap
mechanism_check: The drain hose must not let sink water siphon back into the dishwasher — the air gap (or a high loop) breaks the siphon.
The air gap is a small chrome dome on the sink deck; the hose runs up to it and back down to the disposal or drain.
Supply is hot water through a dedicated stop; the electrical is a separate trade — know the boundary.
improvised_tools: An air gap fitting (or plan a high loop secured under the countertop).
Hose clamps and a 90-degree dishwasher elbow for the supply.
steps: Mount the air gap in the sink deck hole; run the dishwasher drain hose up to it with no sags.
Run the second hose from the air gap down to the disposal inlet (knock out the disposal plug first) or the drain tailpiece.
Connect the hot supply through the shutoff to the dishwasher inlet with a new braided line.
Run a full cycle and check all three connections dry — supply, drain, and air gap.
stop_conditions: If there is no accessible shutoff for the dishwasher supply, add one first — never hard-pipe a dishwasher you cannot isolate.
Electrical hookup beyond a plug-in cord is electrician territory — stop at the water connections if you are not qualified.

title: Replace a saddle valve with a proper tee valve
mechanism_check: A saddle valve pierces the pipe with a needle and clamps on — it leaks, clogs, and violates code in most places.
The honest fix is cutting in a tee with a real quarter-turn valve: full-bore, serviceable, legal.
This is the classic previous-guy repair — budget extra time for corroded pipe around the saddle.
improvised_tools: A tee fitting plus a quarter-turn ball valve (sweat, compression, or push-fit to match your skill).
A tubing cutter and deburring tool.
steps: Shut the main, drain the line, and remove the saddle valve.
Cut out the pierced section — the needle hole never seals again.
Install the tee and valve with your chosen joining method; support the new valve.
Pressurize, check, and cap or connect the outlet line.
stop_conditions: If the pipe around the saddle is deeply pitted, cut further back to sound pipe — do not valve onto rot.
If the line is old galvanized steel, stop: threading or transitioning galvanized is its own job — plan it separately.

title: Flush sediment from a water heater
mechanism_check: Sediment settles on the tank bottom, insulates the burner or element, and causes popping, inefficiency, and premature tank death.
The drain valve at the tank base is the flush path; the cold inlet is the refill.
Draining a tank with the power or gas still on destroys elements and overheats the tank.
improvised_tools: A garden hose long enough to reach a drain or outside.
A bucket to inspect what comes out — sandy grit means the flush was overdue.
steps: For electric: kill the breaker. For gas: set to pilot. Then shut the cold inlet.
Hook the hose to the drain valve, run it to a safe drain, and open a hot faucet somewhere to vent.
Open the drain valve and flush until the water runs clear — pulse the cold inlet a few times to stir the sediment.
Close the drain, refill fully (steady water at the open hot faucet), then restore power or full gas.
stop_conditions: If the drain valve is plastic, ancient, and will not open — or snaps — stop: replacing a drain valve on a full tank is a pro job.
If the tank is over 12 years old and has never been flushed, weigh replacement over flushing: disturbing a decade of sediment can finish a dying tank.

title: Relight a gas water heater pilot
mechanism_check: The pilot heats a thermocouple that holds the gas valve open; no pilot, no thermocouple signal, no gas — that is the safety.
The control knob has OFF, PILOT, and ON; the pilot position bypasses the safety just long enough to light.
Gas you can smell is gas you respect: if it smells strongly, you do not light anything.
improvised_tools: A long lighter or match — never a short one near the burner chamber.
The heater's own lighting instructions, usually on a label behind the access panel.
steps: Turn the control to OFF and wait five full minutes for any gas to clear.
Turn to PILOT, press and hold the knob, and light the pilot through the access.
Keep holding 30 to 60 seconds so the thermocouple heats, then release — the pilot should stay lit.
Turn to ON and confirm the main burner lights; if the pilot will not stay lit after three tries, the thermocouple is suspect.
stop_conditions: If you smell strong gas at any point, stop: leave the area and call the gas company — no relight is worth the risk.
If the pilot lights but dies repeatedly, stop replacing your patience: the thermocouple or gas valve needs a pro.

title: Test a water heater T and P relief valve
mechanism_check: The temperature-and-pressure relief valve is the tank's last defense: it opens if heat or pressure runs away.
A working valve snaps open and reseats; a dead one is either seized shut (dangerous) or weeps constantly (failed).
Test it yearly; replace it the moment it misbehaves — this is a safety device, not a convenience.
improvised_tools: A bucket under the discharge pipe — it will spit hot water.
A replacement T and P valve on hand, because testing sometimes finishes a weak one.
steps: Confirm the discharge pipe runs down to within inches of the floor and is not capped.
Lift the test lever briefly: hot water should flow from the discharge pipe, then stop cleanly when you release.
If it weeps afterward, tap the lever once more to reseat it; persistent weeping means replacement.
If nothing comes out, the valve is seized — replace it immediately, do not leave a tank unprotected.
stop_conditions: If the discharge pipe is capped, plugged, or missing, stop using hot water until it is fixed — that is a tank with no safety release.
Replacing a T and P valve means draining below its level and working on a hot tank — if you are not comfortable, call a pro; this one matters.

title: Upgrade washing machine hoses
mechanism_check: Washer hoses see full house pressure 24/7 and fail catastrophically — a burst hose is hundreds of gallons per hour.
Rubber hoses age out in about 5 years; braided stainless lasts far longer but is not immortal.
The failure is always at the crimp or the washer — inspect both ends, not the middle.
improvised_tools: Braided stainless hoses (or auto-shutoff FloodSafe style) in the right length.
New rubber washers — the old ones are compressed flat.
steps: Shut both washer stops, run a drain cycle to relieve pressure, and unscrew the old hoses.
Inspect the valve threads; replace any cracked plastic outlet.
Hand-thread the new hoses with fresh washers, then snug a quarter turn — over-tightening cracks the valve.
Open the valves, run a fill, and check both ends; leave the valves accessible, not buried behind the machine.
stop_conditions: If the shutoff valves leak or will not close, replace them first — new hoses on bad valves still flood.
If the drain standpipe overflows during the test fill, stop: that is a drain capacity problem, not a hose problem.

title: Winterize an outdoor hose bibb
mechanism_check: A frost-free sillcock shuts off 12 inches inside the warm wall; a standard bibb shuts off at the cold wall face.
Trapped water freezes, expands, and splits the pipe inside the wall — the leak shows up in spring.
Disconnecting the hose is 80 percent of winterizing: a connected hose traps water in any bibb.
improvised_tools: A foam faucet cover for exposed bibbs.
The interior shutoff for the bibb line, if one exists.
steps: Disconnect every hose, splitter, and timer — nothing stays connected past the first freeze.
If there is an interior shutoff, close it and open the outside bibb to drain the line.
Leave the outside bibb open at 45 degrees over winter so any residual water has room to expand.
Cover exposed bibbs with an insulated cap.
stop_conditions: If the bibb drips from the stem when you touch it in fall, rebuild or replace it now — a weeping bibb freezes into a split pipe.
If the pipe already froze and split inside the wall, stop: that is a cut-and-replace repair, not winterizing.

title: Kill a sewer smell from a dry trap
mechanism_check: Every drain's trap holds a water plug that blocks sewer gas; unused drains (floor drains, guest baths) evaporate dry in weeks.
The smell is sewer gas, not just unpleasant — it is methane and hydrogen sulfide.
Refilling the trap is the fix; keeping it filled is the maintenance.
improvised_tools: Water — a gallon per drain. A tablespoon of mineral oil to slow the next evaporation.
A flashlight to confirm the trap holds water.
steps: Pour a gallon of water into every infrequently used drain — floor drains, guest tubs, basement sinks.
Add a tablespoon of mineral oil to floor drains; it floats on the water and slows evaporation.
Run the guest bathroom fixtures monthly — put it on a calendar.
If the smell persists after refilling, the trap may be siphoned or the vent blocked — that is the next diagnosis.
stop_conditions: If the smell is strong, persistent, and in multiple rooms, stop pouring water and investigate the vent stack or call a pro — a blocked vent siphons traps dry.
If you smell gas (rotten eggs) near a gas appliance rather than a drain, that is the gas company, not plumbing.

title: Replace a water heater anode rod
mechanism_check: The anode rod is a sacrificial magnesium or aluminum metal: it corrodes so the steel tank does not.
When it is consumed, the tank starts corroding — checking it every few years doubles tank life.
It is threaded into the tank top and often seized; the tank must be held still while you break it free.
improvised_tools: A 1-1/16 inch socket with a breaker bar (or an impact wrench).
A second person or a strap to keep the tank from twisting.
Teflon tape for the new rod's threads.
steps: Kill power or gas, shut the cold inlet, and relieve pressure via a hot faucet.
Break the old rod free — steady pressure, tank held still; expect it to fight.
Pull it and inspect: less than half an inch of metal left, or coated in calcium, means it was overdue.
Tape the new rod's threads, thread it in snug, refill, and restore power or gas.
stop_conditions: If the tank twists or the top flexes when you torque the rod, stop: you will break a connection — call a pro with the right hold-back.
If the tank is already leaking from the shell, an anode will not save it — replace the heater.

title: Design a PEX home-run manifold system
mechanism_check: A home-run manifold gives every fixture its own dedicated PEX line from a central manifold — no tees hidden in walls, and each fixture gets its own shutoff.
It is a design problem: fixture count, distances, and pressure drop decide the manifold size and layout.
The payoff is serviceability: one leak never requires tearing open a wall to find a buried fitting.
improvised_tools: Graph paper or a sketch app; a fixture list with distances from the manifold location.
Manifold sizing rule of thumb: 3/4-inch trunk, 1/2-inch runs to most fixtures.
steps: List every fixture and measure its run distance from a central, accessible manifold location.
Size the manifold ports to the fixture count plus two spare; plan 3/4-inch for tubs and hose bibbs, 1/2-inch for the rest.
Route each run with gentle bends (no kinks), label both ends, and leave a service loop at the manifold.
Pressure-test the whole system before closing anything up.
stop_conditions: If the design needs more ports than a single manifold offers, do not daisy-chain manifolds awkwardly — redesign the layout or split into zones.
If local code requires accessible shutoffs at each fixture anyway, the manifold is a bonus, not a substitute — check code first.

title: Diagnose before you quote
mechanism_check: Most callbacks come from quoting the symptom instead of the cause: the running toilet that is actually a cracked tank, the clog that is a collapsed line.
Diagnosis is a separate, billable phase — it protects both the plumber and the customer from a wrong fixed price.
Uncertainty is highest at first contact, so the quote must be staged (diagnostic fee, then options), not a single guess.
improvised_tools: A standard diagnostic checklist: what you check, in what order, every time.
A flat diagnostic fee, stated up front — it buys honesty on both sides.
A camera or phone photos to show the customer what you see.
steps: Quote the diagnostic visit as its own line item before you touch a wrench.
Run the full diagnosis (shutoffs, meter, isolation tests) and document findings with photos.
Present the cause, the options (good-better-best), and the price for each — then let the customer choose.
Never start the repair on a verbal just-fix-it without the agreed scope in writing.
stop_conditions: If the customer will not pay for diagnosis, walk away politely — free guesses become free callbacks.
If the diagnosis reveals something outside your license (gas, structural, electrical), stop and refer — do not quote what you cannot legally do.

title: Price a job: flat-rate versus time-and-materials
mechanism_check: Flat-rate pricing sells certainty: the customer pays for the outcome, and your efficiency becomes profit.
Time-and-materials sells honesty on unknowns: the customer pays for what it actually takes, and your risk drops to zero.
The failure mode is mixing them: flat-rate quotes on unknown conditions, or T and M on simple jobs where the customer feels the meter running.
improvised_tools: A personal rate sheet: your hourly cost (wage, truck, insurance, overhead) — most one-truck plumbers underprice because they skip this math.
A flat-rate book for common jobs, built from your own timed history.
A written scope template: what is included, what is not, what triggers a requote.
steps: Compute your true hourly cost first — everything else hangs on this number.
Use flat-rate for known, repeatable jobs (fill valve, wax ring, disposal swap); use T and M for unknowns (leak searches, old-house repipes).
State the trigger conditions in writing: if the flange is broken, the price becomes X.
Review every job against the quote monthly; adjust the book, not your memory.
stop_conditions: If you cannot state your true hourly cost, stop quoting flat-rate — you are guessing, and guesses lose money.
If a job's unknowns exceed what T and M can fairly cover (structural rot, code upgrades), stop and re-scope before continuing.

title: Present good-better-best options honestly
mechanism_check: Customers choose badly when given one take-it-or-leave-it price; they choose well when the trade-offs are visible.
Good-better-best works because it separates the must-fix (safety, code) from the nice-to-have (efficiency, longevity).
The mechanism is trust: the middle option should be what you would buy for your own house.
improvised_tools: A three-tier option sheet: repair, replace, upgrade — each with lifespan and warranty stated.
Photos of the actual condition — the customer cannot evaluate what they cannot see.
steps: Always lead with the repair that solves the immediate problem (the good).
Offer the full replacement with its longer lifespan and warranty (the better — usually your recommendation).
Offer the upgrade path (efficiency, water savings) without pressure (the best).
Let silence do the selling: present, answer questions, and let them choose.
stop_conditions: If the good option is unsafe or violates code, do not offer it — say so plainly and offer only the safe options.
If the customer pushes you to do the cheap option against your judgment, get the refusal of the recommended work in writing.

title: Run a one-truck plumbing operation
mechanism_check: A one-truck shop lives or dies on utilization: windshield time is unpaid, callbacks are double-unpaid.
The truck is a warehouse on wheels — every missing part is a second trip that eats the job's margin.
Standardize the 20 parts that cover 80 percent of calls, and systematize scheduling so the day has a shape.
improvised_tools: A restock checklist tied to the week's jobs — restock Friday, not Monday morning.
Time blocks: mornings for scheduled jobs, afternoons flexed for emergencies.
A simple job log: address, work, parts, time — the data your flat-rate book is built from.
steps: Build the truck stock list from your actual call history; cull anything unused in 90 days.
Batch jobs geographically; never cross town twice for two small calls.
Restock to the checklist every Friday; count the high-turnover parts (supply lines, flappers, fill valves).
Review the job log monthly: which jobs made money, which ate it, and what changes next month.
stop_conditions: If callbacks exceed one in ten jobs, stop adding new customers and fix the quality leak — growth on callbacks is bankruptcy with extra steps.
If you are turning down work for three straight weeks, raise prices before hiring — price is the first lever, headcount is the last.

title: Mentor an apprentice on the job
mechanism_check: Apprentices learn by doing, not watching — but unsupervised doing creates callbacks and hazards.
The mechanism is graduated responsibility: explain, demonstrate, supervise, then release — one skill at a time.
The failure mode is using the apprentice as a parts fetcher for a year, then being surprised they cannot solder.
improvised_tools: A skill ladder: the ordered list of tasks from cut-and-deburr to diagnose-alone.
The teach-back: after showing a task, the apprentice explains it back before touching tools.
A five-minute end-of-day debrief — what went well, what to fix tomorrow.
steps: Start every new skill with the mechanism: why the joint works, before how to make it.
Demonstrate once at full speed, once slowly narrated, then hand over the tools under supervision.
Release tasks in order of reversibility: cutting and cleaning first, soldering and gas last.
Debrief daily; sign off skills on the ladder only when demonstrated twice without coaching.
stop_conditions: If the apprentice is unsafe (torch, gas, electricity-adjacent work) despite coaching, pull them back to supervised tasks — no schedule pressure overrides safety.
If you are explaining the same failure for the third time, stop and change the teaching method, not the apprentice — the lesson is not landing.

title: Grow from apprentice tasks to journeyman judgment
mechanism_check: The apprentice-to-journeyman gap is not skill with tools — it is diagnosis: knowing which problem you are actually looking at.
Judgment is pattern recognition built from varied reps: same symptom, different causes, across many houses.
Deliberate exposure plus reflection builds it — volume alone just rehearses the same five jobs.
improvised_tools: A personal call log: symptom, diagnosis, what you checked, what it actually was.
A mentor or crew to debrief the weird ones with — judgment compounds in conversation.
Code book study in small doses: one section a week beats a cram weekend.
steps: Log every diagnostic call: what you thought, what you tested, what it was.
Review the log monthly for patterns — the misdiagnoses are the curriculum.
Volunteer for the weird calls, not just the fast ones; variety builds the pattern library.
Study for the license in the trade's own language: code sections tied to jobs you have actually done.
stop_conditions: If you are diagnosing by replacing parts until something works, stop and get supervision — that is expensive guessing, not judgment.
If burnout is making you rush diagnoses, say so: rushed judgment is how journeymen create a callbacks worth of rework.

title: Coordinate a two-person rough-in
mechanism_check: Rough-in is parallel work in tight spaces: one person measuring and cutting, one fitting and hanging — collisions waste more time than the work itself.
The coordination challenge is sequencing: the critical path is whoever is waiting on the other.
Verbal callouts replace line-of-sight in walls and crawlspaces — the crew that talks does not redo.
improvised_tools: Role split: cutter-measurer and fitter-hanger, swapped at lunch so both stay sharp.
Callouts: cutting, clear, holding — three words prevent most rework.
A shared cut list on tape or a whiteboard — no measuring twice from memory.
steps: Walk the plan together first: mark every penetration and run on the studs before cutting anything.
Split roles; the fitter never waits — the cut list stays one step ahead.
Call out every cut and every handoff; confirm with a repeat-back in noisy spaces.
Pressure-test or eyeball-check each other's runs before closing — the second pair of eyes is the quality system.
stop_conditions: If the two of you are redoing each other's work, stop and re-walk the plan — the plan is wrong, not the people.
If fatigue has you mismeasuring, call the break: rough-in mistakes get buried in walls.

title: Run an emergency leak call as a crew
mechanism_check: A leak call is triage under time pressure: stop the water, limit damage, then diagnose — in that order.
The failure mode is two people both diagnosing while water keeps flowing.
Roles must be assigned in the truck, before the door opens: one on water, one on damage control.
improvised_tools: Pre-assigned roles: water (shutoffs, main) and salvage (towels, buckets, moving valuables).
A leak-call kit by the door: clamps, rubber, push-fit couplings, towels, headlamps.
A 60-second size-up script: where the water is coming from, where the main is, what is getting damaged.
steps: On arrival, split immediately: one to the main shutoff, one to contain the water.
Size up together for 60 seconds before touching tools — source, spread, and shutoff status.
Stabilize with the fastest reliable repair (push-fit, clamp); diagnose the root cause only after the bleeding stops.
Debrief on the drive back: what slowed you down, what goes in the kit next time.
stop_conditions: If water is near electrical panels or outlets, stop and kill the power first — water plus electricity ends crews.
If the leak is sewage rather than supply water, switch to containment and call for the right equipment — do not improvise with black water.

title: Hand off from rough crew to finish crew
mechanism_check: The handoff is where information dies: the rough crew knows every buried compromise, the finish crew inherits them blind.
Finish problems (misaligned stub-outs, buried valves) are rough decisions made without the finish in mind.
A written, visual record beats memory — memory leaves with the rough crew.
improvised_tools: A handoff sheet: photos of every in-wall run, valve locations, and anything non-standard.
Painter's tape labels on stub-outs: fixture name and height.
A 15-minute walkthrough, rough lead to finish lead, before the rough crew leaves the site.
steps: Rough crew photographs everything before insulation and drywall — no exceptions.
Label every stub-out and valve with tape: what it feeds, and any quirk.
Walk the finish lead through in person; they sign the handoff sheet acknowledging the quirks.
Finish crew verifies measurements against the fixture schedule before setting anything — trust, then verify.
stop_conditions: If the handoff sheet is blank and the rough crew is gone, stop and open-test: pressurize and inspect before closing walls on mystery plumbing.
If stub-outs do not match the fixture schedule, stop setting fixtures — re-rough the misaligned ones rather than forcing trim to fit.

title: Run the tailgate toolbox talk
mechanism_check: Crews repeat the same mistakes because lessons stay in one person's head.
A five-minute talk at the tailgate transfers one lesson to the whole crew, every day — compound interest on experience.
The mechanism is ritual: same time, same place, one topic — low friction beats comprehensive.
improvised_tools: One topic per day, drawn from yesterday's work — real, recent, relevant.
The apprentice teaches one talk a week — teaching is the fastest way to learn.
A notebook of topics covered, so nothing repeats monthly.
steps: Gather at the truck before the first job: one topic, five minutes, everyone standing.
Frame it as a story: what happened, what the mechanism was, what to do next time.
Ask the crew for their version — the best lessons come from the quietest tech.
Log the topic; rotate who leads so it never becomes one person's lecture.
stop_conditions: If the talk becomes a blame session, stop and reset the frame: mechanisms, not people — blame kills the ritual.
If nobody can name a lesson from the last week of talks, the format is stale — change it rather than dropping it.

title: Improvise together when the parts run fails
mechanism_check: The parts run fails when the fitting on the truck does not match the pipe in the wall — now the crew is burning daylight.
Group improvisation beats solo heroics: four eyes see combinations one person misses.
The mechanism is constraint-sharing: state what is on the truck out loud, and the solution usually assembles itself.
improvised_tools: The truck inventory out loud — one person reads what is actually in the bins while the other stares at the problem.
Roles: one holds the problem steady, one hunts parts, one keeps the customer informed.
A phone camera to the supply house: a photo of the pipe end beats three wrong trips.
steps: Stop and state the constraint out loud: what fitting you need, what you actually have.
Inventory the truck verbally — adapters, bushings, and transition fittings hide in forgotten bins.
Design the workaround as a team: sketch it, check each joint's physics, then build it.
Tell the customer what you did and why before you leave — improvised joints get documented, not hidden.
stop_conditions: If the workaround needs more than two adapters stacked, stop: that is a Rube Goldberg joint — make the supply run.
If anyone on the crew is uncomfortable with the workaround's safety, the workaround is vetoed — no majority votes on pressure-containing joints.

title: Leave it clean: the punch-list ritual
mechanism_check: Customers remember the mess longer than the repair — cleanliness is the cheapest marketing a crew has.
The punch-list catches the small failures (drips, uncaulked edges, missing escutcheons) before they become callbacks.
A fixed end-of-job sequence, done the same way every time, so nothing depends on memory at 5 PM.
improvised_tools: A laminated punch card: wipe, check, test, photograph — ticked off, not remembered.
Drop cloths and shoe covers as standard kit, not special requests.
The customer's own eyes: walk them through the finished work.
steps: Test everything you touched: run water, flush, check every joint dry.
Wipe down fixtures, remove all debris and old parts, vacuum the work area.
Walk the customer through: show the repair, explain the warranty, hand over any leftover parts or documentation.
Tick the punch card and photograph the finished work for the job file.
stop_conditions: If you find a drip during the punch check, stop the ritual and fix it — leaving a known drip is how one-star reviews are born.
If the customer is not available for the walkthrough, document with photos and a note — never skip the record.
